newsitem.title: USA: OECD report suggests Fed consider rate rise.
newsitem.headline: OECD report suggests Fed consider rate rise.

text.p: The U.S. economic expansion is expected to slow next year, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development said Tuesday, but warned policymakers to stay alert for signs of inflation.
The OECD, in an annual review of the U.S. economy, estimated that inflation adjusted growth would rise by 2.1 percent in 1997 as against 2.4 percent in the current year.

"The economy is for all intents and purposes at full employment with fairly low inflation and while some risks certainly exist, it looks likely to continue that way over the next two years," the report said.
But it made clear that it might be a good idea for the Federal Reserve to keep interest rate policy firm to help insure that inflation is kept from gathering any strength.

"While the level of interest rates needed to reduce pressures on capacity is uncertain...some insurance against any reemergence of upward trends in inflation should prudently be bought in the form of a monetary stance conducive to slowing the growth of aggregate demand," the OECD said.

While done earlier this year, release of the report by the 28-nation group comes just one day before the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets to decide the course of interest rates. Most analysts believe the Fed will leave them unchanged.
The report was done by the OECD's economic and development review committee, and its forecasts assume that the Fed has kept a rein on policy.
The report estimated that the gross domestic product price deflator, a measure of inflation, would remain unchanged from 1996 levels at 2.1 percent in 1997.

But in making these estimates, the report also said it was crucial that further action be taken to bring the budget into balance with a special effort to reform the Medicare health system and Social Security in light of increased demands from an aging population.

The report, written before the Nov 5 presidential election in which President Clinton won a second term, said any tax cut should be conditioned on actually achieving the spending cuts needed to meet the goal of a balanced budget by 2002.
It noted that official projections already foresee a moderate-sized deficit rise next year even with a complete freeze in discretionary spending and favorable interest rates.
"It is, therefore, crucial that an early start be made to confronting these problems - health care in particular," the report said.
The OECD noted criticism of recent U.S. trade policy while it acknowledged that the country had been a global leader in moving to unrestricted exchange of goods.

"Concern has been expressed in the committee about certain other aspects of recent U.S. trade policy, in particular the recent enactment of the Helms-Burton Act and other similar legislation which extend U.S. law beyond U.S. borders," the report said.
The Helms-Burton Act penalizes foreigners who do business involving property confiscated from Americans in Cuba after communist leader Fidel Castro came to power in 1959.

While conceding that income distribution seems more uneven in the United States than Europe, the report still questioned the decision to raise the minimum wage, arguing that it might hamper employment possibilities for some workers.

"In principle, the committee does not support the recently enacted increase in the minimum wage," the report said, adding, "it is a blunt instrument which may put the least skilled at risk by reducing their job opportunities."
